catalog_quote: Stress in Muyang will not receive major treatment here. The following remarks are based on a brief study of recorded data for nouns. Normal Muyang speech applies relatively great stress to the final syllable of an utterance. This is normally measurable as amplitude and always measurable as length – almost equivalent to doubling the length of the vocalisation of a final syllable. Because of this the normal stress pattern of a word is not properly observable in its isolation form. ... Amplitude and high tone in Muyang are linked. In nouns of three syllables there is a fairly consistent correlation between measurable amplitude and pitch, high tone receiving greater force in utterance. However, the utterance-final stress pattern overrides this, giving greater force to a word-final low tone that to preceding higher tones. new_statements.quote: Normal Muyang speech applies relatively great stress to the final syllable of an utterance. This is normally measurable as amplitude and always measurable as length ... Because of this the normal stress pattern of a word is not properly observable in its isolation form. [...] Amplitude and high tone in Muyang are linked. [...] It may be, therefore, that if stress is relevant at word-level at all, it is closely linked to tone. Nouns of two syllables starting with high tone have a tendency to break the link between tone and amplitude, suggesting that there may be an overriding tendency towards word-final stress in disyllabic nouns. [...] With the exception of the utterance-final increase, stress in general may not prove to be a significant factor in Muyang.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Muyang is a tone language (three surface level tones H/M/L, perhaps two underlying). Prominence (amplitude and especially length) falls on the final syllable of the utterance, which masks any word-level pattern in citation forms; within nouns amplitude tracks High tone, with a possible tendency to word-final stress in disyllabic nouns; the author concludes stress is probably not a significant independent factor at word level, pending further research.
new_statements.exceptions: Utterance-final stress overrides the tone-amplitude correlation (a word-final Low gets more force than preceding Highs); disyllabic H-initial nouns tend toward word-final stress; remarks based only on recorded nouns.
new_statements.domain_note: The firm statement is utterance/phrase-level (final syllable of the utterance); word-level stress explicitly left undetermined. Isolation (citation) forms show the utterance-final lengthening.
new_statements.identity_note: Smith 1999 describes Muyang as spoken in Guduba (canton of Palbara), Tokombéré, Mayo-Sava, Far North Cameroon; same language as Glottolog muya1243, no dialect split noted. The stress remarks are explicitly 'based on a brief study of recorded data for nouns'.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the same document as the source of the catalog's existing statement (Smith 1999 Muyang Phonology; Glottolog lists it undated). The full scanned confirms the existing quote verbatim and adds the conclusion sentence on p.52 ('Stress is important at phrase level, probably less so at word level') and the p.17 aside that a full vowel in a closed final syllable carries stress. Same reading: tone language with a stress statement, prominence utterance-final, no word-stress rule asserted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Muyang has three level surface tones (H, M, L; p.27) and lexical tone on nouns. Prominence (amplitude + roughly doubled length) falls on the last syllable of the utterance, i.e. it is a phrase-level, not word-level, phenomenon. Within nouns, amplitude follows high tone; the author doubts that word-level stress exists at all, with at most a tendency to word-final stress in disyllabic nouns. Conclusion p.52: 'Stress is important at phrase level, probably less so at word level.'
new_statements.exceptions: Utterance-final stress overrides the tone-amplitude link, giving a word-final low tone more force than preceding higher tones; where a word has no prominent high tone there is no prominent amplitude pattern either; disyllabic nouns beginning with high tone tend to break the tone-amplitude link (possible word-final stress). p.17 (PDF p.18) remarks in passing that a full vowel in a closed final syllable 'in these cases also carries stress'. The author states the remarks rest on 'a brief study of recorded data for nouns' and that further research is needed before word-level stress can be discounted.
new_statements.identity_note: Smith 1999 describes the Muyang of the arrondissement of Tokombéré, department of Mayo-Sava, Far North Province, Cameroon (cantons Palbara and Mouyengué), based on work with speakers Djeved François and Aviwai (p.4); no dialect distinction is made. Glottolog's 'Smith (n.d.) Muyang phonology, 53 pp.' and the catalog's 'Smith 1999 Muyang Phonology' are one and the same document (title page: 'Muyang Phonology, Tony Smith, 1999, SIL BP 1299 Yaoundé').

sources.note: Ch. 5 'Stress' (p.30): utterance-final syllable receives great stress (amplitude, ~doubled length), so a word's own stress pattern is not observable in isolation; in nouns amplitude correlates with High tone; disyllabic nouns show a tendency to word-final stress; concludes stress 'may not prove to be a significant factor', word-level stress not yet established. Ch. 4: three surface level tones H, M, L (possibly two underlying).
